blocks.text: Born in New York in 1947, Stephen Shore is one of the photographers who made color a serious medium in American art. He was 14 when Edward Steichen bought three of his prints for the Museum of Modern Art, and still a teenager when he photographed daily life at Andy Warhol’s Factory. In 1971, the Metropolitan Museum of Art gave him a solo show, making him the first living photographer exhibited there since Alfred Stieglitz. The following year, he crossed the United States with a small 35mm camera for “American Surfaces,” a visual diary of diners, motel rooms, meals and strangers. He then switched to an 8×10 view camera for the road trips that became Uncommon Places (1982), a landmark of the New Color generation. Shore has directed the photography program at Bard College since 1982, and his book The Nature of Photographs remains a reference for students worldwide.

On the occasion of his retrospective “Véhiculaire & Vernaculaire,” which was held at the Fondation Henri Cartier-Bresson in Paris in 2024, Stephen Shore took part in a public conversation with Quentin Bajac, director of the Jeu de Paume, held in the heart of the exhibition. Bajac knows the work closely: as chief curator of photography at the Museum of Modern Art, he organized Shore’s first career-spanning survey in the United States in 2017.
